title: Net Toolbox
summary: The tools you reach for when the network misbehaves: a step-by-step diagnosis, ping, traceroute, DNS lookup, port check, HTTP check, a speed test with a needle gauge, public IP, whois, Wake-on-LAN, a Bluetooth radar, Local devices (a LAN scanner), Wi-Fi networks with their channels, a Wi-Fi walk test and the interfaces.
description: A full-screen network toolbox made for the deck's small screen and for touch. Diagnosis answers 'why is my internet broken?' in plain words, step by step: link, address, gateway, DNS, internet and a captive-portal check (a plain HTTP request to connectivitycheck.gstatic.com/generate_204). Ping shows every packet (ok, slow or lost), the loss, min/avg/max and the jitter; it needs no root (an unprivileged ICMP socket, allowed by net.ipv4.ping_group_range on Raspberry Pi OS). DNS lookup asks for A, AAAA, MX, TXT, NS or PTR records through the system's resolver, a typed one or 1.1.1.1, 8.8.8.8 and 9.9.9.9, and shows the CNAME chain, the answer time and the response code. Port check tells whether a TCP port of a host is open, closed or filtered, with presets for web, mail, SSH, DNS and remote desktop. Traceroute draws the path to a host as a chain of hops with a latency bar and a loss tag each, in rounds like mtr, with no root (a silent hop is shown as normal, a hop that only limits its answers is told apart from real loss). HTTP check makes one request with curl and shows the status, the timing as a waterfall (DNS, connect, TLS, waiting, transfer) and the days left of the site's certificate; ignoring certificate errors is an explicit switch. Public IP shows the address the internet sees (through Cloudflare's trace page) and says when your provider shares it between customers. Whois asks IANA and the registry it names (TCP port 43) and summarises the answer. Speed test measures download, upload, latency and jitter against Cloudflare's speed.cloudflare.com on a needle gauge with a live throughput chart, then grades the latency under load from A to F (bufferbloat); it uses at most 150 MB each way, only when you press Start, and says so (on a phone hotspot that is mobile data). Wake-on-LAN keeps up to 20 saved machines, sends the magic packet through the network you chose and watches the machine's address for up to two minutes, showing in a ring and a strip of seconds when it wakes up. Bluetooth radar scans for the devices around with BlueZ and draws them as blips on near, medium and far rings (signal strength, not distance) with a list and the details of each device; Wi-Fi and Bluetooth share one radio, so a Bluetooth keyboard may stutter while it scans, and it needs the bluez package. Local devices (it replaces LAN Scan) scans your own network without root and lists what answers, as it is found: the address, the name (mDNS, NetBIOS or reverse DNS), the MAC, the vendor (a random address is shown as private), the round trip, the router and this device marked; a device's page pings it, checks a port, scans its common ports or ports 1 to 1024 (only devices of your own network can be scanned) and saves it for Wake-on-LAN. Wi-Fi networks (it replaces Wi-Fi Survey) lists the networks around with signal bars, channel, band and security in plain words, a page per network with its vendor and what its security means, and a Channels view that names the least crowded channel of 2.4 and 5 GHz; it asks NetworkManager for its own scan and never connects to anything, so it needs the network-manager package. The Wi-Fi walk test draws the signal against time while you walk with the board, with a weak-zone line you can set (-70, -75 or -80 dBm), marks the weak readings and the access point changes, and ends with a summary: the weakest spot and when, the average, the time in the weak zone, the dips. Interfaces lists each adapter with its state, addresses, MAC, speed, the gateway, the DNS servers and the Wi-Fi network. Every result can be saved as text to ~/net-logs. Nothing leaves the board until you start a test. Works on the Pi Zero 2 W, Pi 3A+, Pi 5 and CM5. Rows show what can be tapped: a chevron opens or changes, a dot runs. Needs a screen of at least 640x480 and a launcher with full-screen app support.
depends: libfreetype6, libinput10, libxkbcommon0, curl, ca-certificates, network-manager
